Holt Communication Station Pine Gap Scroll down Video credit: The Australian Ministry of Defence In the near pitch blackness of a wet June morning, a US B-2 Spirit stealth bomber swoops from the sky, touching down on the outskirts of Brisbane to swiftly refuel – engines still running – at one of the US air force’s key allied bases. Before the sun is up, the nuclear-capable warplane is back in the air. RAAF Base Amberley, about 50km south-west of Brisbane, is a vital staging point for US military operations across the region. But it is hardly alone. This map shows every military base in Australia, which includes US- and Australian-run bases. Analysts warn of a “saturation” of the continent by the US military, and argue that Australia’s most important security ally could drag the country unwillingly into war. Amid the red dirt of Katherine, the runway at RAAF Base Tindal is being expanded to be able to better accommodate massive American B-52 bombers, the so-called “Stratofortresses”. These aircraft are able to land on Australian soil carrying nuclear weapons. The US government won’t tell Australia if and when they are. The Australian government won’t ask. On the remote coast of Western Australia, a cluster of highly technological assets – deep space radar, space surveillance telescope, and the Harold Holt naval communication station – provide vital information to enable US submarine and space warfare. The naval communication station is designed to reach submerged submarines. Its antenna array broadcasts on very low frequency radio. The US-run Pine Gap, in the centre of the country, is regarded by some as the US military’s most valuable intelligence site outside the continental United States. The satellite tracking and signals intelligence base detects missile launches, intercepts military communications and provides targeting information for US forces around the world. Essentially incorruptible – difficult to access, physically or otherwise – in a desert valley in the centre of a massive continent, it downloads and transmits masses of data from powerful US satellites constantly monitoring vast swathes of the globe. For the US military, Australia represents, in the words of one now-retired general, “location, location, location”. Australian military The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war? Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here US military presence in Australia, mapped – video Why can the US access so many Australian military bases? – podcast Ben Doherty , Andy Ball and Nick Evershed Sun 6 Sep 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 17.35 EDT Share US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent. New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18. In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia. “We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces … “But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.” The US military-industrial complex in Australia Each square represents one facility United States-controlled facilities with Australian access (17) Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access (24) Australian facilities with US military access (51) Australian facilities with US corporate access (18) Australian facilities with no significant US access (41) Australian facilities with US access unresolved (17) US access to Australian defence facilities Access level Facilities United States-controlled facilities with Australian access 17 Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access 24 Australian facilities with US military access 51 Australian facilities with US corporate access 18 Australian facilities with no significant US access 41 Australian facilities with US access unresolved 17 Guardian graphic ‘Aligning ourselves completely’ The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for: Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts. Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory. Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft. Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific. Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified. Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known. Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles , stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific. 7:00 US military presence in Australia, mapped – video Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe. Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “ promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says. Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view. Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications. View image in fullscreen Workers with a missile at the Port Wakefield facility. Photograph: Lockheed Martin The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities. Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American. The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft. The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication. This is a massive institutional failure in Australia Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”. “From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean. “For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.” Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne , says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone. Is Australia at war with Iran? The fine line between ‘defensive operations’ and complicity Read more “Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China , springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning. “From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.” There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting. Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult. “This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.” View map of military facilities by the numbers ‘Waltzing its way into a war’ At a press conference in June , the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia. Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria. “We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said. View image in fullscreen US defense secretary Pete Hegseth meets Australia’s defence minister Richard Marles at the Pentagon. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”. Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region. “We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.” Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “ agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases , bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”. The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory. But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”. The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said. Australians’ fragile faith Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents . But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing. A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history. Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet. a graphic Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%). Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security. Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%). More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally. Explore the US military's footprint in Australia Australian facility Australian facility with US military access Australian facility with US access unresolved US facility with Australian access US corporate access All bases Australian US Facility type: All types ▾ Guardian graphic This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once- great and powerful friend . “After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.” Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran. “Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets. “It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane , and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.” Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”. “Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.” Secret documents reveal preferred Australian nuclear submarine base – and warn it could be a military target Read more She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate ,

Photograph: Lucas Neves/NurPhoto/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Flávio Bolsonaro speaks to the media in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. Photograph: Lucas Neves/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Brazil Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say Far-right senator and his family boarded private plane to Ecuador after crossing border to Argentina, Argentina’s government confirms Tiago Rogero in Brasília and Tom Phillips in São Paulo Wed 28 Oct 2026 02.36 EDT First published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who called the act “shameful”. A report by the news website Metrópoles , citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from. Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added. Argentina’s government confirmed that Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters had crossed the border into Argentina and boarded a private flight to Ecuador, at 11.30pm on Tuesday night. “They did so with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment to entering the country,” Argentina’s National Directorate of Migration said on X. “Furthermore, the transits were recorded by the competent authority without incident.” The flight, the agency said, was operated by the company Baires Fly S.A. and bound for Guayaquil, 260km (160 miles) south-west of the Ecuadorian capital, Quito. The Bolsonaros entered Argentina via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing in the province of Misiones, it added. Lula condemned Bolsonaro’s apparent decision to flee. “This is what the family Bolsonaro are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he’s become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília. “I keep imagining what’s on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful.” Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that Bolsonaro was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”. “They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added. The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning. A US state department spokesperson said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted visas “to allow them entry into the United States”. Lawmakers from Lula’s Workers’ party asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list. Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday. A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”. A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear. Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country. The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off. It is unclear if that flight was the same plane the Bolsonaros used to flee to Ecuador. How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil Read more Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Lula, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.” One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost. The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US. As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country. The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies. The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear. Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case. Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right. “The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said. Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement. Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties. “I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas. Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run. Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth. Speaking in Brasília, Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of his candidate’s departure. “Because yesterday we talked about the need for Flávio, with the 60m votes he received, to take on this role as leader of the opposition … since we were given a mandate by a significant part of the population,” he said. Asked whether he believed Bolsonaro could lead the opposition from abroad, he said: “María Corina Machado did it” with her country, Venezuela. Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations. Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen. Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother. “Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist. https://hvg.hu/itthon/20261110_videki-pr.text: A Vidéki Prókátorként ismert Fülöp Botond ügyvéd szerint Lajtár Istvánnak csak az ügyészség tekintélyébe sikerült még egyet belerúgnia, amikor a kamaránál bepanaszolta az ukrán pénzszállítók, majd Fürcht Pál ügyvédjeként ismert Horváth Lórántot, aki ellen fegyelmi eljárás is indult. Az ügyészség alacsony társadalmi megbecsültségéért, az ügyészségbe vetett közbizalom megingásáért azok a felelősök, akik az ügyészséget az elmúlt 16 évben vezették, élükön Polt Péterrel – írta kedd délutáni Facebook-bejegyzésében a kegyelmi ügyet kirobbantó Vidéki Prókátor, vagyis Fülöp Botond ügyvéd, miután kiderült, hogy a Legfőbb Ügyészség amiatt panaszolta be Horváth Lóránt ügyvédet a Budapesti Ügyvédi Kamaránál, mert Horváth élesen bírálta az ügyészség működését. Horváth Lórántot a közvélemény előbb a magyar hatóságok által feltartóztatott, majd a gyanú szerint jogellenesen fogva tartott ukrán pénzszállítók, később az ügyészségen belül érvényesülő nyomásgyakorlásokról beszámoló Fürcht Pál volt főügyész ügyvédjeként ismerhette meg. Horváthot októberben az akkor átmenetileg éppen Lajtár István legfőbbügyész-helyettes által vezetett Legfőbb Ügyészség panaszolta be a fővárosi kamaránál. Azt kifogásolták, hogy az általa vitt ügyekkel kapcsolatban olyan nyilatkozatokat tesz a médiában, amelyek alkalmasak az ügyészség tekintélyének és a szervezetbe vetett társadalmi bizalomnak az aláásására. A panasz nyomán most indult előzetes fegyelmi eljárás Horváth Lóránt ellen. Ez azért is érdekes, mert a Budapesti Ügyvédi Kamaránál a héten tartanak választást, amelyen a szervezet 8 éve regnáló jelenlegi elnökének éppen Horváth az egyik kihívója. Horváth Lóránt ügyvéddel szemben a Legfőbb Ügyészség tett bejelentést októberben, mondván, hogy nyilatkozatai megingatják az ügyészségbe vetett társadalmi bizalmat. Az előzetes eljárást pár nappal a kamarai választás előtt indították el, ahol Horváth a jelenlegi elnök kihívója. Fülöp Botond szerint azonban már az sincs rendben, ha a Legfőbb Ügyészség azért igyekszik meghurcolni egy ügyvédet, mert az nyilvánosan kritizálja a működését. Őszintén szólva nem értem, hogy a Legfőbb Ügyészség honnét vezette le az ügyvédek általi bírálhatatlanságának követelményét – fogalmazott az ügyvéd, leszögezve, hogy a vádhatóság vezetői is kötelesek tűrni a bírálatot. Fülöp Botond a korábbi ügyészségi vezetéssel szembeni kritika megalapozottságára is kitért posztjában: „Nem a tükör a hibás, hanem az arc, melyet mutat” – írta, megjegyezve, hogy tetszik, vagy nem tetszik: ügyészi közreműködés nélkül nem jöhetett volna létre maffiaállam – szögezte le. Arra is emlékeztetett, hogy 16 éven keresztül „menetrendszerűen siklottak ki a hatalomhoz tartozók elleni eljárások”, amelyek aztán a rendszerváltást követően indultak csak meg. Ezek után szerinte ismét csak az ügyészség tekintélyének árt, hogy a szervezet vezetése megpróbálja meghurcolni az őket kritizáló ügyvédet.
